reviews.one_line_contribution: That outcome-based per-item utility scores in agent experience banks are confounded with how often an item's task family appears in the stream, so cap-bounded utility pruning silently strips rare-family coverage — invisible on stationary evaluation, costly after a shift toward those families — and that dividing utility by family exposure (or pruning by redundancy) at the same cap removes most of the cost.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two threats, both verified via the literature command (s2cli / Semantic Scholar + HF). (1) arXiv:1911.05248, 'What Do Compressed Deep Neural Networks Forget?' (with arXiv:2010.03058, 'Characterising Bias in Compressed Models', which the automated novelty card also surfaced at sim 0.42): the exact epistemic claim — pruning leaves top-line accuracy intact while concentrating essentially all the damage on the long tail, so aggregate metrics hide it — and the same class of fix (arXiv:2310.20673 constrains disparate subgroup impact during sparsification; cf. arXiv:2605.08137 for the LLM version). The proposal's contribution is that result ported from weights to external experience items, with 'distribution shift' substituted for 'tail subset'; it cites none of this literature, and a reviewer who knows it will read the hypothesis as a substrate transfer rather than a new phenomenon. The same argument holds a third time in continual learning, where the failure of loss/utility-based buffer selection under class imbalance is the founding motivation for class-balanced reservoir sampling (my search returned adjacent recent work, e.g. arXiv:2602.23834, which reports class-balanced selective replay under temporal drift). (2) arXiv:2604.12007, 'When to Forget: A Memory Governance Primitive' — verified; the proposal declares this ID 'not found on either channel'. It formalizes exactly the estimator under attack, proving multiplicative-weights retention converges to p+(m) = Pr[success | m retrieved] under a *stationary retrieval regime with a minimum exploration condition*. The conditional-on-retrieval estimand and the explicit stationarity/exploration caveat are the proposal's diagnosis stated as a theorem; what remains genuinely unclaimed is the empirical per-family survival and post-shift cost measurement. Neither work makes the proposal's full claim in the agent-memory substrate, so this is not a collision, but together they cap conceptual novelty low.
reviews.strongest_objection: The design cannot separate the claimed frequency *confound* from ordinary estimator *variance*, and under the stream as specified the headline result is close to arithmetic. Rare items are admitted rarely (phase A: 900 tasks x 0.06 x 2 families x success rate yields on the order of a few dozen rare-family admissions) and are retrieved rarely, so their success-minus-failure counters and outcome-credited EMAs are estimated from a handful of uses and are high-variance. Any noisy score with a bottom-rank eviction rule deletes low-count items preferentially — that is a small-sample/shrinkage failure, not evidence that utility is 'frequency in disguise', and every prediction P1-P4 is satisfied by the variance mechanism alone. P4 in particular does not discriminate: random pruning is uniform, so 'utility pruning loses only on rare families' follows from count-driven noise exactly as it follows from a frequency confound. Relatedly, the proposal's own decomposition is under-identified: with six families at two exposure levels (0.22, 0.06), 'Spearman correlation between per-item utility and family frequency' has a predictor with two distinct values and six independent units, so the pre-registered threshold rho >= 0.4 over items is a two-group difference reported with item-level degrees of freedom, and the leave-one-out per-use control is itself estimated on a 150-task probe with almost no rare-family coverage. Second-order but real: P3's 3-null-SD gate against a 100-task per-family held-out set demands roughly a 12-15 point rare-family drop before anything counts, which the proposal flags in Risk Factors and then does not resolve in the budget; and the primary contrast is against the *unbounded* bank (a), which is not cap-matched, so 'post-shift loss relative to (a)' mixes coverage loss with bank size.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Break the confound/variance tie explicitly rather than assuming the confound: add a shrinkage or UCB-style retention rule (hierarchical prior over per-family per-use value, or eviction on the upper confidence bound of utility rather than the point estimate) as a third fix alongside frequency normalization and redundancy — if the shrinkage estimator recovers the rare-family gap, the story is estimator variance and the title claim is wrong; if only exposure normalization recovers it, the frequency confound is established. Make exposure continuous instead of binary: give the six families a graded weight profile (e.g. a Zipf-like ladder) so utility-vs-exposure is a real regression with per-family random effects, and report the partial effect at the family level, not a Spearman over items. Move the headline comparison to the cap-matched set (b)/(c)/(d) vs (e)/(f)/(g) and keep the unbounded bank as context only. Reconcile power with the gate: either raise per-family held-out sets until the MDE reaches the 3-SD threshold, or drop to a paired per-item difference statistic with a pre-registered smaller effect. Finally, cite and dispatch the compression-bias precedent (1911.05248 / 2010.03058 / 2310.20673) directly — say what an experience store makes different from a sparsified network — and re-run the collision check, since arXiv:2604.12007 is retrievable in one query and is the closest formal statement of the mechanism.
reviews.missing_baseline: A variance-corrected utility estimator at the same cap — Bayesian shrinkage toward a family-level prior, or eviction on a lower/upper confidence bound rather than the raw counter/EMA. Without it, every predicted result is explainable by low-count noise in rare items' utility estimates and the frequency-confound interpretation is unearned. Secondarily, arXiv:2604.12007's multiplicative-weights retention primitive belongs in the policy set as the published forgetting rule whose stationarity assumption the paper claims to break (the proposal already plans to add RoMeRL, arXiv:2608.02508, as an estimator variant, which is the right instinct); and there is no cap-matched coverage-maximizing control (family-stratified reservoir/quota) separate from the frequency-normalized utility, which is the standard continual-learning answer and would show whether utility information contributes anything beyond stratification.
reviews.preprint_collision: No verified collision. But the check is materially defective on its own terms. It reports that arXiv:2604.12007 was 'not found on either channel'; I ran `s2cli.py paper 2604.12007` (channel: literature command / Semantic Scholar) and it resolves immediately as 'When to Forget: A Memory Governance Primitive' (2026-04-13, 1 citation), proving MW retention converges to Pr[success | m retrieved] under a stationary retrieval regime — the most on-point item in the proposal's own list, dismissed as unverifiable. The check also spends its first two searches on WebSearch, exhausts that budget, and never searches the model-compression or replay-buffer literature where this claim already exists in another substrate. My queries, all on the literature command (Semantic Scholar + HF Papers), no WebSearch used: (1) 'utility-based pruning of agent experience memory deletes rare task coverage frequency bias' -> arXiv:2608.08389 (marginal-value pruning of research-agent tokens), 2607.01444, 2605.24941, 2605.12493, 2602.06052, 2512.16962, 2509.25140, 2306.07929 — none measures a frequency confound or post-shift collateral cost; (2) same mechanism restricted to the last twelve months (--recent) 'memory pruning collateral forgetting rare task distribution shift agent experience bank' -> arXiv:2606.16285 (HiMPO, credit-assignment leakage in memory), 2606.05684, 2606.04536, 2605.04811, 2605.12493, 2509.25140 — no collision; (3) closest named method, 'ReMe procedural memory refinement pruning low-utility entries agent evolution' -> confirms ReMe arXiv:2512.10696 plus ProcMEM 2602.01869, MemPro 2606.00619, EvoAgentBench 2607.05202, Memp 2508.06433 — none runs a shift test or per-family survival analysis, so the proposal's characterization of ReMe holds; (4) 'pruning disproportionately harms long-tail rare subgroups compression identified exemplars aggregate accuracy hides' -> arXiv:1911.05248, 2010.03058, 2310.20673, 2605.08137 — the claim's structure already published for weight pruning, uncited; (5) 'class-balanced replay buffer rare class forgetting continual learning' -> arXiv:2602.23834 and older CL work (a more literal first attempt returned empty; reported as empty). IDs verified by `s2cli.py paper`: 2512.10696 (ReMe), 2601.03192 (MemRL, 83 cit), 2601.18642 (FadeMem — the 'active forgetting/differential decay' description is fair), 2605.09315 (CPE), 2604.27003 (When Continual Learning Moves to Memory), 2512.11485 (Mistake Notebook Learning), 2607.13591 (MemCon), 2608.02508 (RoMeRL), 2505.16067 (ACL 2025, 90 cit), 2604.12007 (contra the proposal), 2601.19199 (MAGNET), 2608.30177 (Stage-Wise Utility-Risk), 2603.15642 (CraniMem). All thirteen resolved; none failed verification.
